Here's a nice linkage concerning Riviera hot spots...In the autumn of 1922, a few months after Ulysses came out, James Joyce went to Nice with Nora and their daughter Lucia. He meant to rest, but a serious attack of his eye trouble kept him there for several weeks, and he spent the time in bed or in a doctor’s care. The family went back to Paris in November. None of the FAM had a nice time there.

Many scholars think that the germination of the "work in progress" that became Finnegans Wake, took place during his bedridden days on the Riviera. Some of his earliest notes for the book date to that time, and he wrote its first actual drafts in early 1923 -- it was not published until 1939. Incidentally, the first American publication of Ulysses didn't happen till 1934, when a judge declared at trial that its Iewd scenes were NOT NAUGHTY.

I’m happy to report that I only met FDR once, because the encounter was so unpleasant, so utterly mortifying in fact, that the mere thought of a second meeting brings chills to my spine, even to this day.  The year was 1902, and I was a freshman at Harvard College.  Through my father’s influence, I found myself moving ably among lofty circles of fraternal society in Cambridge that year. Dinners with Dean LeBaron Briggs and faculty from the esteemed philosophy department (including William James and Josiah Royce) were not uncommon. Indeed, I once attended a séance hosted by Harvard President Eliot’s wife Grace, at their home on Quincy Street, which included prominent guests such as Alice Mary Longfellow and Harry Houdini.  In that first year, I was very proud to be “punched,” or invited to attend the final dinner and election of initiates into the Porcellian Club, the oldest, most hallowed and venerable of Harvard’s final clubs.  It was well known on campus that sophomore student Franklin Roosevelt, despite being fifth cousins of then-US President Theodore Roosevelt, who, himself, had been a Porc during his tenure at Harvard, was not invited to the dinner, and thusly rejected from the fraternity outright. It was also understood that this rejection bore young Roosevelt no small measure of painful shame and disgrace.  It was therefore no surprise when he showed up that night to the dinner uninvited, and completely sauced beyond coherency.

So an extremely breezy solve for me, but to be honest—ADAM Driver, Henry FONDA, Raquel WELCH, OTIS Redding, James JOYCE, even JOSIE and the Pussy Cats—I don’t think you can construct a puzzle with more proper nouns that are slam dunk in my wheelhouse better than this.

Two things about Doug Peterson.  

First, one thing that comes out of every puzzle he’s had a hand in is that twinkle in his eye, something that makes you smile.  Could be in clues or theme, but it’s always there.  When I see his name atop a grid, already I’m in a good mood.

Second, he loves to collaborate.  This solo puzzle, in fact, was preceded by 13 he made with others.  Undiluted Doug shows his skill in every aspect of puzzlemaking.  Today, a grid with hardly a whiff of ugliness in answer, plus many words I love: STAID, JETTY, DROLL, SERAPE, FOP, JAMB, MISDEED, REPROOF, RATTLETRAP.

For me, the solve was neither a downhill “Whee!” nor an uphill trudge – perfect Wednesday level.

Doug, you’ve been making Times puzzles for 20 years, and your spark is a vibrant as ever.  You are a Crosslandiia treasure.  Thank you for another splendid outing!

Polish crosswords never drop diacritical marks, but that greatly limits the variety of entries, making the grids dull. I'm here at the NYT daily, but I never solve Polish crosswords.

@Alex you are right regarding the abuse of other languages when stuck with the limited keyboard of the NYT crossword puzzle style. But abusing the languages (as @Andrzej has also commented) is routine here. We cant even agree on simple plurals (🐙🐙🐙🐙) …. 😀

@Alex I emphatically disagree. On the foreign spelling point, if we apply this rule, then these words can never appear in crosswords: Bánh mì, Phở , déjà vu, and many more. I prefer that our puzzles are enriched with words of foreign origin, even if the inability to enter the correct letters may make it appear that the noodle soup pronunciation rhymes with 'no'.

@Alex I also disagree with your punchline comment. Your 'for us' implies that all solvers share your opinion. I, for one, do not. I find some revealers useful for the solve, while I find some fun after the solve, tying together seemingly unrelated fill in an unexpected way. Like today. Fun for me at least.

The trouble is that ñ isn't just an n with an accent in it, it's a separate letter that changes both meaning and pronunciation. All the letters in 'espanol' exist in Spanish, but it's not a Spanish word. You can't compare it to a transliteration of e.g. a Vietnamese word that uses the Latin alphabet with diacritics to approximate pronunciation.
Apart from that, 'pho' is an English word that's in Merriam Webster, 'espanol' isn't a word in any language (I'm aware of).

@CB On the revealer, yes you're right it was quite fun at the end, especially the French Riviera one. I do prefer the kind of theme that's part of the solve as well as just something to notice afterwards, but I'll concede I did like this one and I'll retract that part of my post. Gaydar was very good too :)
Dropping diacritical marks in clues though, that's unforgivable, IMO.
